newsitem.title: GABON: Gabonese vote for new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Gabonese vote for new parliament.

text.p: Gabonese voted on Sunday in much-delayed parliamentary elections under a deal to end political violence stemming from President Omar Bongo's disputed 1993 re-election.
Serious delays, in part due to security forces refusing to hand over voting materials without specific orders, disrupted the start of polling in the capital Libreville.

Long queues formed by the middle of the day in certain parts of the city, where the main opposition National Woodcutters Rally won chaotic local elections in October. Witnesses reported a heavier deployment of security forces than in October.
The elections are part of a democratic timetable brokered in Paris in 1994 after political violence shook the oil-producing Central African nation, killing more than a dozen people.
"These elections are special for us. We want the opposition to take over the government," one 39-year-old woman voter told Reuters.
More than 1,000 candidates were bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly. Gabon, a former French colony of 1.2 million people, has an electorate of 550,000.

Opposition parties, while playing a full part in the elections, have denounced delays in issuing voter cards and displaying electoral lists. Under the electoral law, this must be completed eight days before polling.

Sunday's vote was Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.
Bongo has ruled Gabon since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba.
His Democratic Party was expected to face strong competition from the Woodcutters Rally, led by Father Paul Mba Abessole, a Roman Catholic priest and runner-up in 1993.

That election triggered opposition protests in which at least five people died. Pay protests turned violent and political in early 1994. The official death toll then was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
The head of the electoral commission, Antoine Nguema Essone, told state television late on Saturday the deployment of security forces was to ensure disciplined and peaceful polling.

Electoral commission officials said in Akieni in the south, Bongo's stronghold, voting material had been vandalised and was being replaced by plane as were missing ballot papers for a candidate in Minvoul in opposition territory in the north.

Sunday's polls had been due to open at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT) but election officials said the delays could lead to an extension of voting. Past experience suggests results could take over a week to trickle out.
